# Study roadmap

[English](ROADMAP.md) · [中文](ROADMAP.zh.md)

Five study orders over the same pages, one per track described in the [hiring process guide](PROCESS.md). Pick the track that matches the role you are interviewing for and work down it. ★ shows how often a question comes up, from ★★★★★ (again and again) to ★☆☆☆☆ (rarely).

## Research (RS / RE)

Research scientists and research engineers: a recruiter or team-lead call, skills interviews that mix coding, an oral ML-knowledge round and ML coding or design, then final interviews with team leads, a research talk or paper discussion and behavioural rounds.

### 1 · Before the first call

Motivation comes up in almost every round, and the research conversation decides whether a team wants you. Both take longer to prepare than code, so start them first.

| # | Problem | Priority | Difficulty | In one line |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Recruiter Screen: Motivation, Research Interests and Logistics](behavioral/recruiter-screen/README.md) | ★★★★★ | — | A 30-minute call with a recruiter, not a technical interviewer, that opens on why you want to join Google DeepMind specifically, covers your research interests and which ladder you are applying for, spends about two minutes on your background, and closes on the logistics that let the rest of the process be scheduled: work authorisation, location, timeline, level and compensation. |
| 2 | [Research Deep Dive: Paper Discussion and Research Talk](behavioral/research-deep-dive/README.md) | ★★★★★ | — | A 45-minute paper or project deep dive that goes as deep as the interviewer can take it, or a 45-minute research talk with questions, in which researchers from the team probe the motivation, method, experiments, limitations and your individual contribution behind a piece of your own research, then press on a claimed confound or ask you to critique a published paper, and ask what you would work on next. |

### 2 · The ML-knowledge round

Oral questions answered in a few minutes each, some with a short derivation. Practise saying the answers aloud.

| # | Problem | Priority | Difficulty | In one line |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [ML Fundamentals: Metrics, Losses, Optimisers and Regularisation](quiz/ml-fundamentals/README.md) | ★★★★★ | Medium | Fifteen oral questions on classification metrics, loss gradients and regression losses, generative models, optimiser mechanics, generalisation, and offline-to-online evaluation, each answered with a derivation and checked numerically against a brute force, a simulation, or an independent library. |
| 2 | [LLM Fundamentals: Attention, Transformers and the Training Pipeline](quiz/llm-fundamentals/README.md) | ★★★★★ | Hard | Twelve rapid derivations spanning attention and the LLM training pipeline: the 1/sqrt(d) scaling and attention's compute and memory cost, the KV cache and RoPE, parameter and FLOP counts, pre- versus post-norm, cross-entropy and perplexity, byte-pair encoding, compute-optimal scaling, post-training objectives, sampling, and mixture-of-experts routing, each traced through a worked number. |
| 3 | [RL for Language Models: Policy Gradients, PPO, GRPO and DPO](quiz/rl-for-llms/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Hard | Explain and derive the objectives behind post-training a language model with reinforcement learning: the policy-gradient identity and variance-reducing baselines, PPO's clipped surrogate and generalised advantage estimation, GRPO's group-relative advantage and its two normalisation biases, low-variance KL estimators, the closed-form derivation behind DPO, how reward hacking shows up and is mitigated, and the on-policy/off-policy distinction together with the exponential variance cost of importance-sampling corrections across a response. |
| 4 | [Maths Quiz: Probability, Statistics and Linear Algebra](quiz/maths-probability-linear-algebra/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Twelve rapid derivations spanning probability, statistics and linear algebra: Bayes' theorem on urns and a diagnostic test, waiting times for coin patterns, order statistics of uniform draws, the bias of the Gaussian MLE variance, ridge and lasso as MAP estimates, KL divergence with mode-covering versus mode-seeking fits, the sample size for a confidence interval, SVD versus eigendecomposition and PCA, positive semidefiniteness and convexity, matrix-calculus gradients, and how conditioning governs gradient-descent convergence, each checked numerically. |
| 5 | [Maths Quiz: Matrix Computation, Statistical Tests and Information Theory](quiz/maths-stats-information-theory/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Twelve rapid-fire questions spanning matrix computation, statistics and information theory: the cost and conditioning of matrix multiplication and inversion, the pseudo-inverse, moments and the reach and limits of the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem, hypothesis testing and multiple comparisons, a chi-square goodness-of-fit test, a two-sample Bayes classifier, entropy, cross-entropy and perplexity, mutual information, and a set of integrals by hand, each traced to where it shows up in machine learning and checked numerically. |

### 3 · Core coding

Graph search in its many forms is the most frequent coding topic; the code has to run.

| # | Problem | Priority | Difficulty | In one line |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Warm-Up: Scanning an Array and Traversing a Graph Depth-First](coding/graph-dfs-warmup/README.md) | ★★★★☆ | Easy | Two short warm-ups -- counting array elements above a threshold, then building an undirected graph from an edge list to traverse it depth-first, split it into components and detect a cycle -- that reward speed, precision and stated tie-breaking rules over cleverness. |
| 2 | [Shortest Paths Through Locked Doors](coding/state-space-bfs/README.md) | ★★★★★ | Hard | BFS over a (row, column, keys-held) state space to find, and count, shortest paths through a grid of keys and doors, then extend it to weighted terrain with Dijkstra. |
| 3 | [Most Frequent Events in a Stream](coding/event-frequency-stream/README.md) | ★★★★☆ | Medium | Find the most frequent message and its timestamps in a batch of events, then keep answering the same question after every arrival into a bounded sliding window without ever rescanning it, then track approximate heavy hitters over an unbounded stream with the Space-Saving algorithm and a fixed number of counters. |
| 4 | [Winning Positions in a Token-Moving Game](coding/token-game-outcomes/README.md) | ★★★★☆ | Hard | Reverse-topological minimax finds win/loss outcomes on a DAG, retrograde BFS extends it to graphs with cycles and draws, and Sprague-Grundy numbers decide a game played with several tokens at once. |
| 5 | [Python Generators, Unit Tests and Weighted Sampling](coding/weighted-sampling-generator/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Write a lazy generator over a list with several corner cases and a full unittest suite for it, then a weighted sampler built from prefix sums and binary search, and finally Vose's alias method for O(1)-per-draw sampling, testing randomness with a stub RNG and a chi-square goodness-of-fit check. |
| 6 | [Unit Conversions as a Weighted Graph](coding/unit-conversion-graph/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Model unit-conversion facts as a weighted graph to answer conversion queries, detect the first fact that contradicts the ones before it, and then support an online, interleaved stream of facts and queries with a weighted union-find in near-constant amortised time. |

### 4 · ML coding and debugging

| # | Problem | Priority | Difficulty | In one line |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Attention with a KV Cache and an Online Softmax](coding/attention-kv-cache/README.md) | ★★★★☆ | Hard | Implement causal multi-head attention in NumPy, an incremental KV-cache decoder that reproduces it exactly row by row, and a blockwise attention routine with an online softmax that never materialises the full score matrix, in the style of FlashAttention. |
| 2 | [Debugging a Classifier That Does Not Learn](coding/training-loop-debug/README.md) | ★★★★☆ | Medium | Debug a from-scratch NumPy classifier that runs without crashing yet never learns, tracing six independent bugs in shuffling, softmax, gradient scaling, momentum, dropout and the accuracy metric to their distinct symptoms, then write sanity checks that catch each one before a full training run. |
| 3 | [Backpropagation from Scratch](coding/mlp-backprop-from-scratch/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Derive and implement the forward and backward passes of a two-layer ReLU network with softmax cross-entropy loss, verify every gradient with a central-difference check, and train on a non-linearly-separable dataset to show why He initialisation works and all-zero initialisation cannot. |
| 4 | [EM for a Gaussian Mixture: Derive and Implement](coding/em-gaussian-mixture/README.md) | ★★☆☆☆ | Hard | Derive the E-step and M-step of EM for a Gaussian mixture from Jensen's inequality, implement a numerically stable fit_gmm in NumPy, and connect it to k-means in the small-variance limit and to BIC-based model selection. |
| 5 | [Focal Loss versus Cross-Entropy](coding/focal-loss/README.md) | ★★☆☆☆ | Medium | Derive the focal-loss gradient in closed form, implement it as a numerically stable NumPy function, and measure how much less of the training gradient it hands to easy, already-confident examples than cross-entropy does, on an imbalanced synthetic classification problem. |

### 5 · ML system design

The design round is specific to the team, so also prepare a design in your target team's own area.

| # | Problem | Priority | Difficulty | In one line |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Design an Evaluation System for an LLM Assistant](system-design/llm-evaluation-system/README.md) | ★★★★☆ | Hard | A weekly release gate for a candidate model across 12 task domains: golden-set side-by-side evaluation with a human-calibrated autorater and position-bias cancellation, Bradley–Terry ranking with bootstrap confidence intervals, a Holm-adjusted non-inferiority gate across domains, and synthetic prompts, rubric grading and contamination screening for domains with no labelled data. |
| 2 | [ML Design: Predicting a Reaction Factor for Pairs of Molecules](system-design/molecule-reaction-ml-design/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | A symmetric, order-invariant regression target spanning four orders of magnitude: EDA for replicate noise and pair-order conflicts, order-invariant pair representations built from molecular fingerprints, molecule-disjoint splitting to keep leakage out of the harder evaluation, a model sequence from a per-molecule baseline to a structure-based GNN or transformer pair encoder, and an active-learning loop for choosing which pairs the lab should measure next. |
| 3 | [Training a Model That Does Not Fit on One Accelerator](system-design/distributed-training/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Hard | Design the training run for a 70-billion-parameter transformer across 2,048 accelerators: derive the compute and memory budget, lay out tensor, pipeline and data parallelism with a sharded optimiser, and size checkpointing against stragglers, hardware failures and a mid-run loss spike. |
| 4 | [ML Design: A Data Flywheel for a Robot Manipulation Policy](system-design/robot-learning-data-flywheel/README.md) | ★★☆☆☆ | Hard | Designing the data flywheel behind a fleet-scale vision-language-action policy: data volume and storage for teleoperated demonstrations and autonomous rollouts, an episode data model indexed for curation, a labelling-curation-training-evaluation-canary pipeline that turns interventions into DAgger-style training data, Wilson-interval and two-proportion-test statistics for deciding whether a candidate policy actually improved, and the safety limits and action-chunking latency budget that let it serve the fleet. |
| 5 | [ML Design: Predicting Which Data-Centre Machines Need Replacing](system-design/datacentre-failure-ml-design/README.md) | ★★☆☆☆ | Medium | A weekly ranked list of data-centre machines likely to need hardware replacement: leakage-free label and split construction under censoring, feature transforms and machine-type embeddings across three model families, a discrete-time hazard model with a down-sampling correction derived from the odds, and the capacity-bound precision/recall evaluation and feedback loop that keep the ranking trustworthy in production. |

### 6 · Final interviews

| # | Problem | Priority | Difficulty | In one line |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Team-Lead and Hiring-Manager Interviews: Experience, Research Taste and Fit](behavioral/team-lead-rounds/README.md) | ★★★★☆ | — | One or two 45-minute conversations, each with a team lead or with the hiring manager of the specific team, plus future teammates, that go deep on your own experience and how you run an ML experiment, probe your research taste and what you would work on here, check your working style on a research team, can include open-ended questions specific to the team's domain — from the state of today's systems to a product's business case — and close on fit, ramp-up and your own questions — after which the team holds its own debrief on whether it wants you and at what scope. |
| 2 | [Googleyness, Leadership and Culture: Competency Questions](behavioral/googleyness-and-culture/README.md) | ★★★★★ | — | A 45-minute, final-stage competency interview run by a people-and-culture partner or another interviewer trained on the "Googleyness and leadership" rubric, covering motivation and mission, collaboration and conflict, ownership under ambiguity, leadership and teams, failure and feedback, and responsibility. Most questions are answered as one real story in Situation, Task, Action, Result (STAR) form, naming your own specific actions, the evidence of their impact, and what you learned; a few ask instead for a stated position backed by one concrete example. |
| 3 | [Code Review: Ranking the Defects in a Checkpointing Change](coding/code-review-round/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Review a pull request that adds checkpointing and sharded sampling to a training loop, rank its defects by blast radius, then fix and test the ones that can silently lose or corrupt a run. |

### 7 · More coding and code reading

| # | Problem | Priority | Difficulty | In one line |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Painting a Fence with the Fewest Strokes](coding/fence-painting-strokes/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Paint every cell of a row of unit-width planks with as few strokes as possible: horizontal strokes alone reduce to a closed-form sum that a single plank's height change updates in O(1), and allowing vertical strokes too turns the problem into a divide-and-conquer recursion on the range minimum, proved optimal by an exchange argument. |
| 2 | [Bit-Packing Encoders and Decoders](coding/bit-packing-codec/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Pack integers into fixed-width bit fields with a derived byte-length formula, encode signed integers as zigzag-mapped LEB128 varints, and build a frame-of-reference block codec that is chosen over plain varints exactly when it encodes a given block smaller. |
| 3 | [Snapshot Array: History, Compaction and Diffs](coding/snapshot-array/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Build a versioned array that answers a point-in-time read in O(log s) time after an O(1) snapshot, using a per-index change history and binary search; then let old snapshots be released so memory shrinks, comparing an eager sweep against a lazy one with an amortised background pass; then answer a diff between two snapshots in time proportional only to what changed, using a per-interval journal. |
| 4 | [k-d Tree: Nearest Neighbours and Range Queries](coding/kd-tree-nearest-neighbour/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Hard | Build a balanced k-d tree over points in R^d with an explicit median-split rule and a derived height bound, search it for the nearest neighbour and the k nearest neighbours with branch-and-bound pruning whose interaction with tied distances is derived precisely, and count points inside an axis-aligned box in sublinear time using per-node subtree sizes. |
| 5 | [Binary Search on Bitonic Arrays and Monotone Functions](coding/binary-search-monotone/README.md) | ★★☆☆☆ | Medium | Binary-search the peak of a bitonic array in O(log n) and invert a strictly increasing integer function by exponential (galloping) search with no assumed bound on the answer; then handle plateaus with an adversary lower bound and derive the evaluation count and exact floating-point termination for bisecting a continuous monotone function. |
| 6 | [Code Comprehension: What Does This Code Compute?](quiz/code-comprehension/README.md) | ★★☆☆☆ | Medium | Eight short, un-run Python snippets from ML code — a hand-written 1-D convolution and its padded and dilated variants, log-sum-exp, Welford's streaming variance, causal attention masking, reservoir sampling and a pairwise distance matrix — each read aloud, explained precisely, and then checked against a formula, a library implementation or an independent brute force. |

### 4 · System design

| # | Problem | Priority | Difficulty | In one line |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Design the Gemini App](system-design/gemini-app/README.md) | ★★★★☆ | Hard | Design the backend of a multi-turn, multimodal chat assistant that streams token by token at scale, covering context assembly and prefix caching, resumable streaming, safety filtering of a response in flight, model routing under overload, and per-user quotas. |
| 2 | [Design a Retrieval-Augmented Agent over Company Documents](system-design/rag-agent-platform/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Hard | Designs a multi-tenant retrieval-augmented agent over company documents: a chunked, product-quantised vector index sized for 2.2 billion chunks, ACL pre-filtering that a post-filtered top-k cannot substitute for, hybrid BM25-and-dense retrieval fused by reciprocal rank fusion and re-ranked by a cross-encoder, a budgeted multi-step tool loop, and layered defences against prompt injection and data exfiltration. |
| 3 | [Design a Recommendation System for a Content Feed](system-design/recommendation-system/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | A personalised short-video feed: two-tower candidate retrieval over a sharded ANN index, a multi-task ranking model that turns several predicted engagement signals into one score, diversity- and freshness-aware re-ranking, and the negative sampling, delayed-feedback labelling, cold-start handling and exposure-bias corrections that keep the whole loop optimising for long-term satisfaction rather than raw engagement. |

| 5 | [Unit Conversions as a Weighted Graph](coding/unit-conversion-graph/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Model unit-conversion facts as a weighted graph to answer conversion queries, detect the first fact that contradicts the ones before it, and then support an online, interleaved stream of facts and queries with a weighted union-find in near-constant amortised time. |

### 4 · ML coding and debugging

| # | Problem | Priority | Difficulty | In one line |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Debugging a Classifier That Does Not Learn](coding/training-loop-debug/README.md) | ★★★★☆ | Medium | Debug a from-scratch NumPy classifier that runs without crashing yet never learns, tracing six independent bugs in shuffling, softmax, gradient scaling, momentum, dropout and the accuracy metric to their distinct symptoms, then write sanity checks that catch each one before a full training run. |
| 2 | [Attention with a KV Cache and an Online Softmax](coding/attention-kv-cache/README.md) | ★★★★☆ | Hard | Implement causal multi-head attention in NumPy, an incremental KV-cache decoder that reproduces it exactly row by row, and a blockwise attention routine with an online softmax that never materialises the full score matrix, in the style of FlashAttention. |
| 3 | [Focal Loss versus Cross-Entropy](coding/focal-loss/README.md) | ★★☆☆☆ | Medium | Derive the focal-loss gradient in closed form, implement it as a numerically stable NumPy function, and measure how much less of the training gradient it hands to easy, already-confident examples than cross-entropy does, on an imbalanced synthetic classification problem. |

### 5 · System design

| # | Problem | Priority | Difficulty | In one line |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Design a Retrieval-Augmented Agent over Company Documents](system-design/rag-agent-platform/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Hard | Designs a multi-tenant retrieval-augmented agent over company documents: a chunked, product-quantised vector index sized for 2.2 billion chunks, ACL pre-filtering that a post-filtered top-k cannot substitute for, hybrid BM25-and-dense retrieval fused by reciprocal rank fusion and re-ranked by a cross-encoder, a budgeted multi-step tool loop, and layered defences against prompt injection and data exfiltration. |
| 2 | [Design an Evaluation System for an LLM Assistant](system-design/llm-evaluation-system/README.md) | ★★★★☆ | Hard | A weekly release gate for a candidate model across 12 task domains: golden-set side-by-side evaluation with a human-calibrated autorater and position-bias cancellation, Bradley–Terry ranking with bootstrap confidence intervals, a Holm-adjusted non-inferiority gate across domains, and synthetic prompts, rubric grading and contamination screening for domains with no labelled data. |
| 3 | [Design the Gemini App](system-design/gemini-app/README.md) | ★★★★☆ | Hard | Design the backend of a multi-turn, multimodal chat assistant that streams token by token at scale, covering context assembly and prefix caching, resumable streaming, safety filtering of a response in flight, model routing under overload, and per-user quotas. |
| 4 | [Design a Recommendation System for a Content Feed](system-design/recommendation-system/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | A personalised short-video feed: two-tower candidate retrieval over a sharded ANN index, a multi-task ranking model that turns several predicted engagement signals into one score, diversity- and freshness-aware re-ranking, and the negative sampling, delayed-feedback labelling, cold-start handling and exposure-bias corrections that keep the whole loop optimising for long-term satisfaction rather than raw engagement. |
| 5 | [ML Design: Predicting a Reaction Factor for Pairs of Molecules](system-design/molecule-reaction-ml-design/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | A symmetric, order-invariant regression target spanning four orders of magnitude: EDA for replicate noise and pair-order conflicts, order-invariant pair representations built from molecular fingerprints, molecule-disjoint splitting to keep leakage out of the harder evaluation, a model sequence from a per-molecule baseline to a structure-based GNN or transformer pair encoder, and an active-learning loop for choosing which pairs the lab should measure next. |
| 6 | [ML Design: Predicting Which Data-Centre Machines Need Replacing](system-design/datacentre-failure-ml-design/README.md) | ★★☆☆☆ | Medium | A weekly ranked list of data-centre machines likely to need hardware replacement: leakage-free label and split construction under censoring, feature transforms and machine-type embeddings across three model families, a discrete-time hazard model with a down-sampling correction derived from the odds, and the capacity-bound precision/recall evaluation and feedback loop that keep the ranking trustworthy in production. |

### 6 · Final interviews

| # | Problem | Priority | Difficulty | In one line |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Googleyness, Leadership and Culture: Competency Questions](behavioral/googleyness-and-culture/README.md) | ★★★★★ | — | A 45-minute, final-stage competency interview run by a people-and-culture partner or another interviewer trained on the "Googleyness and leadership" rubric, covering motivation and mission, collaboration and conflict, ownership under ambiguity, leadership and teams, failure and feedback, and responsibility. Most questions are answered as one real story in Situation, Task, Action, Result (STAR) form, naming your own specific actions, the evidence of their impact, and what you learned; a few ask instead for a stated position backed by one concrete example. |
| 2 | [Team-Lead and Hiring-Manager Interviews: Experience, Research Taste and Fit](behavioral/team-lead-rounds/README.md) | ★★★★☆ | — | One or two 45-minute conversations, each with a team lead or with the hiring manager of the specific team, plus future teammates, that go deep on your own experience and how you run an ML experiment, probe your research taste and what you would work on here, check your working style on a research team, can include open-ended questions specific to the team's domain — from the state of today's systems to a product's business case — and close on fit, ramp-up and your own questions — after which the team holds its own debrief on whether it wants you and at what scope. |

## Student Researcher and internships

Student researcher positions are decided mainly by a research conversation and a conversation with the host; some loops add a fundamentals round, and software-engineering internships add coding.

### 1 · The research conversation

| # | Problem | Priority | Difficulty | In one line |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Research Deep Dive: Paper Discussion and Research Talk](behavioral/research-deep-dive/README.md) | ★★★★★ | — | A 45-minute paper or project deep dive that goes as deep as the interviewer can take it, or a 45-minute research talk with questions, in which researchers from the team probe the motivation, method, experiments, limitations and your individual contribution behind a piece of your own research, then press on a claimed confound or ask you to critique a published paper, and ask what you would work on next. |
| 2 | [Recruiter Screen: Motivation, Research Interests and Logistics](behavioral/recruiter-screen/README.md) | ★★★★★ | — | A 30-minute call with a recruiter, not a technical interviewer, that opens on why you want to join Google DeepMind specifically, covers your research interests and which ladder you are applying for, spends about two minutes on your background, and closes on the logistics that let the rest of the process be scheduled: work authorisation, location, timeline, level and compensation. |

### 2 · Fundamentals

| # | Problem | Priority | Difficulty | In one line |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [ML Fundamentals: Metrics, Losses, Optimisers and Regularisation](quiz/ml-fundamentals/README.md) | ★★★★★ | Medium | Fifteen oral questions on classification metrics, loss gradients and regression losses, generative models, optimiser mechanics, generalisation, and offline-to-online evaluation, each answered with a derivation and checked numerically against a brute force, a simulation, or an independent library. |
| 2 | [LLM Fundamentals: Attention, Transformers and the Training Pipeline](quiz/llm-fundamentals/README.md) | ★★★★★ | Hard | Twelve rapid derivations spanning attention and the LLM training pipeline: the 1/sqrt(d) scaling and attention's compute and memory cost, the KV cache and RoPE, parameter and FLOP counts, pre- versus post-norm, cross-entropy and perplexity, byte-pair encoding, compute-optimal scaling, post-training objectives, sampling, and mixture-of-experts routing, each traced through a worked number. |
| 3 | [Maths Quiz: Probability, Statistics and Linear Algebra](quiz/maths-probability-linear-algebra/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Twelve rapid derivations spanning probability, statistics and linear algebra: Bayes' theorem on urns and a diagnostic test, waiting times for coin patterns, order statistics of uniform draws, the bias of the Gaussian MLE variance, ridge and lasso as MAP estimates, KL divergence with mode-covering versus mode-seeking fits, the sample size for a confidence interval, SVD versus eigendecomposition and PCA, positive semidefiniteness and convexity, matrix-calculus gradients, and how conditioning governs gradient-descent convergence, each checked numerically. |
| 4 | [Maths Quiz: Matrix Computation, Statistical Tests and Information Theory](quiz/maths-stats-information-theory/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Twelve rapid-fire questions spanning matrix computation, statistics and information theory: the cost and conditioning of matrix multiplication and inversion, the pseudo-inverse, moments and the reach and limits of the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem, hypothesis testing and multiple comparisons, a chi-square goodness-of-fit test, a two-sample Bayes classifier, entropy, cross-entropy and perplexity, mutual information, and a set of integrals by hand, each traced to where it shows up in machine learning and checked numerically. |
| 5 | [CS Fundamentals Quiz: Memory, Concurrency and Floating Point](quiz/cs-fundamentals/README.md) | ★★☆☆☆ | Medium | Ten oral questions spanning object orientation, stack/heap allocation and reference-cycle garbage collection, race conditions and deadlock, the GIL, cache locality, IEEE 754 floating point and bf16/fp16 training precision, and amortised hash-table resizing, each checked by simulation, exhaustive enumeration or a counting model rather than a stopwatch. |
| 6 | [Code Comprehension: What Does This Code Compute?](quiz/code-comprehension/README.md) | ★★☆☆☆ | Medium | Eight short, un-run Python snippets from ML code — a hand-written 1-D convolution and its padded and dilated variants, log-sum-exp, Welford's streaming variance, causal attention masking, reservoir sampling and a pairwise distance matrix — each read aloud, explained precisely, and then checked against a formula, a library implementation or an independent brute force. |

### 3 · Coding, for internships that include it

| # | Problem | Priority | Difficulty | In one line |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Warm-Up: Scanning an Array and Traversing a Graph Depth-First](coding/graph-dfs-warmup/README.md) | ★★★★☆ | Easy | Two short warm-ups -- counting array elements above a threshold, then building an undirected graph from an edge list to traverse it depth-first, split it into components and detect a cycle -- that reward speed, precision and stated tie-breaking rules over cleverness. |
| 2 | [Python Generators, Unit Tests and Weighted Sampling](coding/weighted-sampling-generator/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Write a lazy generator over a list with several corner cases and a full unittest suite for it, then a weighted sampler built from prefix sums and binary search, and finally Vose's alias method for O(1)-per-draw sampling, testing randomness with a stub RNG and a chi-square goodness-of-fit check. |
| 3 | [Shortest Paths Through Locked Doors](coding/state-space-bfs/README.md) | ★★★★★ | Hard | BFS over a (row, column, keys-held) state space to find, and count, shortest paths through a grid of keys and doors, then extend it to weighted terrain with Dijkstra. |
| 4 | [Unit Conversions as a Weighted Graph](coding/unit-conversion-graph/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Model unit-conversion facts as a weighted graph to answer conversion queries, detect the first fact that contradicts the ones before it, and then support an online, interleaved stream of facts and queries with a weighted union-find in near-constant amortised time. |
| 5 | [Bit-Packing Encoders and Decoders](coding/bit-packing-codec/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Pack integers into fixed-width bit fields with a derived byte-length formula, encode signed integers as zigzag-mapped LEB128 varints, and build a frame-of-reference block codec that is chosen over plain varints exactly when it encodes a given block smaller. |
| 6 | [Backpropagation from Scratch](coding/mlp-backprop-from-scratch/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | Medium | Derive and implement the forward and backward passes of a two-layer ReLU network with softmax cross-entropy loss, verify every gradient with a central-difference check, and train on a non-linearly-separable dataset to show why He initialisation works and all-zero initialisation cannot. |

## Product management (PM)

Product managers: a recruiter screen, hiring-manager conversations and a final loop of product, design, execution and AI deep-dive interviews. Every page tagged for product managers or for all roles, highest priority first.

| 1 | [Recruiter Screen: Motivation, Research Interests and Logistics](behavioral/recruiter-screen/README.md) | ★★★★★ | — | A 30-minute call with a recruiter, not a technical interviewer, that opens on why you want to join Google DeepMind specifically, covers your research interests and which ladder you are applying for, spends about two minutes on your background, and closes on the logistics that let the rest of the process be scheduled: work authorisation, location, timeline, level and compensation. |
| 2 | [Googleyness, Leadership and Culture: Competency Questions](behavioral/googleyness-and-culture/README.md) | ★★★★★ | — | A 45-minute, final-stage competency interview run by a people-and-culture partner or another interviewer trained on the "Googleyness and leadership" rubric, covering motivation and mission, collaboration and conflict, ownership under ambiguity, leadership and teams, failure and feedback, and responsibility. Most questions are answered as one real story in Situation, Task, Action, Result (STAR) form, naming your own specific actions, the evidence of their impact, and what you learned; a few ask instead for a stated position backed by one concrete example. |
| 3 | [Product Manager Loop: AI Product Sense and the AI Deep Dive](behavioral/pm-ai-product-sense/README.md) | ★★★☆☆ | — | A product-manager loop of hiring-manager screens and the final loop's four to six 45-minute rounds, each led by a different specialist — a product director, a UX lead, an engineer, sometimes a further director conversation — in which a case about a hypothetical AI product tests your strategy and prioritisation, your grasp of agent metrics and the risk of shipping high-stakes actions, your read of ambiguous user feedback, your design judgement under model latency and multimodality, and, in a closing conversation, your motivation for the specific team. |
